newsitem.title: USA: Gigante guilty of running NYC crime family.
newsitem.headline: Gigante guilty of running NYC crime family.

text.p: A jury on Friday found Vincent "The Chin" Gigante, considered the last of New York's old-time Mafia dons, guilty of racketeering, conspiring to murder other mobsters and running the Genovese crime family.

Gigante, 69, who faces the possibility of life in prison, looked up but showed no emotion as the verdict was read in Brooklyn federal court. He was given 24 hours to turn himself in at a federal prison hospital facility in North Carolina.
Defence attorneys claim Gigante has been incapacitated by mental illness and heart disease for many years. He attended the trial in a wheelchair, often muttering to himself.
But prosecutors say he is a shrewd organised crime boss who has faked illness in hopes of avoiding prosecution.

The jury deliberated for three days before finding Gigante guilty of, among other crimes, plotting to kill Gambino godfather John Gotti. That slaying was never carried out, and Gotti is now in prison for murder and racketeering.
Gigante also was convicted of bid-rigging.
However, the jury failed to find him guilty of the seven murder charges contained in the 21-count federal indictment. Most of those murders related to a dispute with organised crime in Philadelphia.

The prosecution's case against Gigante relied heavily on the testimony of six former mobsters who became government informants, including Salvatore "Sammy the Bull" Gravano, whose testimony was critical in the 1992 Gotti conviction.

Gigante's defence attorneys did not call a single witness on his behalf. They claimed the government informants were induced to lie and said another mobster, Anthony "Fat Tony" Salerno, was convicted of running the Genovese family in 1986.
The conviction comes seven years after Gigante was first arrested. In that time, his attorneys argued he was mentally ill and unable to stand trial.
Gigante earned the nickname "The Oddfather" for his habit of wandering the neighbourhood around his Greenwich Village apartment in a tattered bathrobe and slippers.
